title: Symmetric Tree
directAnswer: A tree is symmetric when its left and right subtrees are mirror images. Don't traverse one tree — compare two pointers walking in opposite directions: `left.left` against `right.right` and `left.right` against `right.left`. The recursive `isMirror(a, b)` is four lines; the iterative version pairs nodes in a queue and pulls them out two at a time. Both run in O(n) time.

remember.pattern: Mirror comparison of two subtrees (outer-vs-outer, inner-vs-inner)
remember.formula:
isMirror(a, b):
    if a == null and b == null: return true
    if a == null or  b == null: return false
    return a.val == b.val
        and isMirror(a.left,  b.right)   # outer pair
        and isMirror(a.right, b.left)    # inner pair
rules: Symmetry is a **two-tree** problem, not a one-tree traversal — compare `root.left` with `root.right`, never `root` with itself.
The mirror crossing is the whole trick: pair `a.left` with **`b.right`** and `a.right` with **`b.left`**. Pairing same-side children silently tests *sameness*, not *symmetry*.
Handle the **both-null** base case before the **one-null** case, or you dereference a missing child.
Compare `a.val == b.val` **and** recurse — a value match alone is necessary but not sufficient.
The iterative form enqueues nodes **in mirror order** (a.left, b.right, a.right, b.left) and dequeues them in pairs.
whenToUse: Asked whether a tree is a mirror of itself around the center
You need to compare two structures position-by-position in reverse
Any 'is this palindromic / reflected' question on a tree shape
Follow-up to Same Tree where one side is flipped
antiSignals: You only have one subtree to inspect → that's a plain traversal, not a mirror check
Order doesn't matter, only the set of values → sort/compare multisets instead
You need the mirrored *tree* as output, not a boolean → that's Invert Binary Tree
Comparison is structural-identical, not reflected → that's Same Tree (a.left vs b.left)
remember.takeaway: Symmetric Tree is Same Tree with a twist: instead of comparing matching sides, you compare crossed sides. Internalize that mirror means outer-with-outer and inner-with-inner, and the entire family of mirror/reflection problems collapses into one four-line helper.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize symmetry as a comparison between two pointers rather than a single traversal, and whether you get the mirror crossing (left.left↔right.right, left.right↔right.left) correct instead of accidentally writing Same Tree.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing same-side children (a.left with b.left), which checks whether the subtrees are identical rather than mirrored — passes [1,2,2] but wrongly handles [1,2,2,3,4,4,3] vs structurally-different inputs.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that this is Same Tree with crossed recursion, then offer the iterative BFS variant unprompted and note both are O(n) time and O(h) / O(w) space respectively.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, check whether it is a **mirror of itself** (i.e., symmetric around its center).

A tree is symmetric if the left subtree is a mirror reflection of the right subtree: the structures match and the values match when one side is read left-to-right and the other right-to-left.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000]
Follow-up: solve it both recursively and iteratively
understanding: We are not traversing a single tree and checking some property of each node. We are comparing two subtrees — the left and the right — to confirm one is the reflection of the other. Reflection means the outermost nodes pair up, the next-outermost pair up, and so on, with matching values at every paired position.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does symmetry require matching values, or only matching structure?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both. The shapes must mirror AND the paired values must be equal. [1,2,2,null,3,null,3] is structurally a mirror but the 3s land on the same side, so it is NOT symmetric.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraint says at least 1 node, but a clean solution treats an empty tree as trivially symmetric (two null children mirror each other).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want recursive or iterative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lead with the recursive mirror helper (cleanest), then offer the iterative BFS version since 'solve it iteratively' is the stated follow-up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could values repeat across the tree?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That's exactly why a value match alone isn't enough — you must also confirm the mirrored positions line up.

examples.explanation: Left subtree is (2 → 3,4), right subtree is (2 → 4,3). Reading the right side in reverse gives 3,4 — a perfect mirror of the left.
Both 2s have a single child, but the left's child is on the right and the right's child is also on the right. They don't mirror — the 3s should land on opposite sides.
A single node has two empty subtrees, which trivially mirror each other.

approaches.name: Recursive Mirror Comparison
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. Frame it as 'compare two pointers walking in opposite directions' — that one sentence is what the interviewer wants to hear.
hints: Symmetry is about the left subtree reflecting the right. So you're really comparing TWO trees, not inspecting one. What two nodes should you start the comparison with?
Write a helper isMirror(a, b). When are two nodes a valid mirror pair? Their values must match, and their children must mirror — but which child of a pairs with which child of b?
The outer edges pair up and the inner edges pair up: a.left mirrors b.right, and a.right mirrors b.left. Recurse on those two crossed pairs.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited at most once as part of exactly one mirror pair, so the work is O(n). The recursion depth equals the tree height h → O(h) call-stack space, O(log n) balanced and O(n) for a degenerate tree.
approaches.explanation:
The reframe that unlocks this problem: symmetry is not a property you can read off a single node, it's a relationship between two subtrees. So we throw away the instinct to traverse `root` and instead launch a comparison of `root.left` against `root.right`, asking at every step 'are these two nodes a valid mirror pair?'

**The base cases come first, and order matters.** Two null nodes are a valid mirror pair — two missing subtrees reflect each other perfectly, so return `true`. If exactly one is null, the shapes already disagree, so return `false`. Checking **both-null before one-null** is what prevents you from dereferencing a node that doesn't exist; flip them and you'd ask `a.val` on a null `a`.

**The crossing is the entire algorithm.** Once both nodes exist, their values must be equal, and then — here is the only line people get wrong — the *outer* children must mirror and the *inner* children must mirror. Concretely `a.left` pairs with `b.right` (the two outermost branches) and `a.right` pairs with `b.left` (the two innermost branches). If you instead recurse on `a.left` vs `b.left`, you've written Same Tree: you'd be checking whether the two subtrees are *identical*, not *reflected*. They happen to give the same answer on a fully balanced value set, which is exactly why the bug survives shallow testing and then fails on the classic `[1,2,2,null,3,null,3]`.

**Why a value match alone isn't enough.** Equality of `a.val` and `b.val` is necessary but not sufficient — the structure underneath has to mirror too. That's why the return statement is a conjunction: value equality `&&` outer mirror `&&` inner mirror. Short-circuit evaluation means the moment any pair disagrees, the whole recursion collapses back to `false` without exploring the rest.

**Why O(n) is the floor.** To certify symmetry you must inspect every node — a single mismatched leaf buried deep can break it — so no algorithm can do better than linear time. The only axis left to optimize is space, which the iterative variant trades from implicit call stack to an explicit queue.
approaches.insight: Symmetric Tree is literally Same Tree with the recursion crossed. If you've memorized `isSameTree`, you get this for free by swapping the second recursive call's argument from `b.left` to `b.right` and `b.right` to `b.left`. Saying that out loud signals you see the shared skeleton beneath both problems.

Checking one-null before both-null, causing a null dereference.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS with a Queue of Pairs
approaches.whenToMention: Offer it when the interviewer says 'now do it without recursion', or to preempt the follow-up. Emphasize you enqueue nodes in mirror order.
hints: Recursion uses the call stack to remember which pairs still need comparing. To remove recursion, store those pairs yourself — in what structure, and what do you store in it?
Use a queue (or stack) of NODES, but enqueue them in mirror order so that when you pull two out, they're the pair to compare.
Each iteration dequeues two nodes a and b, checks the same base cases and value equality, then enqueues the outer pair (a.left, b.right) and inner pair (a.right, b.left).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every node enters and leaves the queue once → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level's worth of node pairs, so its size is bounded by the tree width w → O(w) space, which is O(n) in the worst (bottom-heavy) level but typically less than the recursion's O(h) on skewed trees.
approaches.explanation:
The recursive solution leans on the language runtime's call stack to remember which mirror pairs are still outstanding. The iterative version makes that bookkeeping explicit with a queue, which is the standard answer to 'solve it without recursion' and also sidesteps stack-overflow on pathologically deep trees.

**The key idea is to enqueue in mirror order.** We seed the queue with `root.left` and `root.right`. Then each loop turn pulls *two* nodes — `a` and `b` — that are supposed to be a mirror pair. We run exactly the same checks as the recursion: both null is fine and we `continue`; one null means asymmetry and we return `false`; unequal values mean asymmetry. If they pass, we push the next pairs to compare — and the order we push them in is everything.

**Why the push order is (a.left, b.right, a.right, b.left).** Because we dequeue two at a time, the pairing is determined entirely by insertion order. Pushing `a.left` then `b.right` means the next-but-one dequeue yields exactly that outer pair; pushing `a.right` then `b.left` queues up the inner pair. Get this order wrong and you'll silently compare the wrong nodes — the iterative analog of the same-side bug in the recursion.

**Why a queue and a stack both work.** The comparison is order-independent across pairs: a tree is symmetric only if *every* pair matches, so it doesn't matter whether we process pairs breadth-first (queue) or depth-first (stack). People reach for a queue out of habit, but swapping `ArrayDeque.poll`/`offer` for `push`/`pop` changes nothing about correctness. The only observable difference is the traversal order and thus the peak container size.

**Space trade-off worth stating.** Recursion costs O(h); BFS costs O(w), the maximum level width. On a deep, skinny tree the iterative version actually uses *less* peak memory and avoids stack overflow; on a wide, shallow tree recursion wins. Mentioning this trade-off — rather than claiming one is universally better — is what separates a memorized answer from understanding.
approaches.insight: The whole iterative trick is 'enqueue in the order you'd recurse'. Because we dequeue pairs, the insertion sequence (outer-a, outer-b, inner-a, inner-b) hard-codes the mirror crossing into the data structure instead of into recursive call arguments. Same logic, relocated from the stack frame to the queue.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def isSymmetric(self, root: TreeNode) -> bool:
    if root is None:
        return True
    queue = deque([root.left, root.right])
    while queue:
        a = queue.popleft()
        b = queue.popleft()
        if a is None and b is None:   # matched empties
            continue
        if a is None or b is None:    # shape mismatch
            return False
        if a.val != b.val:            # value mismatch
            return False
        queue.append(a.left)          # outer pair...
        queue.append(b.right)
        queue.append(a.right)         # inner pair...
        queue.append(b.left)
    return True

java.explanation: Seed with the two subtrees that must mirror — left and right of the root.
Pull the two halves of a mirror pair out together — the second poll on the next line completes the pair.
Both empty → this pair is fine, move on (analog of the recursive both-null base case).
Outer pair: enqueue a.left then b.right so they come out together later — this insertion order encodes the mirror crossing.
Completes the inner pair (a.right, b.left). The four offers per iteration are the iterative form of the two crossed recursive calls.

python.explanation: Seed the queue with the two subtrees that must reflect each other.
Dequeue the first half of a mirror pair; the next line grabs its partner.

python.explanation: Matched empties — skip to the next pair.
Outer pair start: a.left will be compared against b.right enqueued next.
Finishes the inner pair (a.right, b.left); push order is what preserves the crossing.

edgeCases.behavior: Seed queue with (null, null); first iteration both-null → continue, queue empties → return true.
Outer pair (2,2) ok, but then a one-null pair appears → return false. Tests that value match alone doesn't save an asymmetric shape.
Queue width peaks at the widest level (~n/2 nodes), so peak space is O(n) here but the algorithm short-circuits the instant any pair mismatches.

pitfalls: Enqueuing in same-side order (a.left, b.left, ...) — reproduces the Same Tree bug.
Polling only one node per iteration instead of two — breaks the pair invariant.
Forgetting the both-null `continue`, then dereferencing null on the value check.
Assuming a queue is required — a stack works identically since all pairs must match.

commonMistakes: Comparing same-side children (a.left vs b.left) — that's Same Tree, not a mirror check.
Checking the one-null case before the both-null case, causing a null dereference.
Returning true on value equality alone without recursing into both child pairs.
Enqueuing nodes in the wrong order in the iterative version, breaking the mirror pairing.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Same-side recursion (writing Same Tree by accident)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Symmetry requires crossing the children. Recursing a.left vs b.left and a.right vs b.right tests whether the two subtrees are identical, not mirrored. It passes balanced inputs but fails cases like [1,2,2,null,3,null,3].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Null checks in the wrong order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you test 'exactly one null' before 'both null', the both-null case is fine — but reversing it the other way and then accessing a.val before any null check dereferences a missing node.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong enqueue order in the iterative version
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Because nodes are dequeued two at a time, the insertion order defines the pairing. Pushing same-side children means you later compare a.left with b.left — the iterative form of the Same Tree bug.

followupVariations.title: Same Tree
followupVariations.hint: The non-crossed sibling of this problem — compare a.left with b.left and a.right with b.right.

followupVariations.title: Invert Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Produces the mirror tree as output; a symmetric tree equals its own inversion.

followupVariations.title: Flip Equivalent Binary Trees
followupVariations.hint: Generalizes the crossing — at each node, try both the matched and the flipped pairing.

followupVariations.title: Subtree of Another Tree
followupVariations.hint: Reuses the same-tree comparison helper as a building block while scanning every node.

patternNote: Two-pointer mirror comparison on a tree. Recognise it whenever you must verify a reflected/palindromic relationship between two subtrees. It's the crossed-recursion cousin of Same Tree, and the same isMirror/isSame helper underlies Subtree of Another Tree and Flip Equivalent Binary Trees.
